title: Crime Aid

jokes.text: I thought about selling a kidney, but Michael offered to get me a part-time job at corporate.
jokes.setup: Pam explains she ran out of money in New York and considered drastic measures like selling a kidney.
jokes.punchline: The punchline is that Michael's 'help' is positioned as barely preferable to organ harvesting — implying working for Michael is its own kind of ordeal.
jokes.explanation: Strong opening confessional. The joke earns its laugh because it's rooted in Pam's specific relationship with Michael — the kidney option is absurd, but the real absurdity is that Michael's 'help' is the lesser evil. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Of course, now Michael knows where to reach me 16 to 18 hours a week.
jokes.setup: Pam got a part-time job at corporate, framed as a solution to her money problems.
jokes.punchline: The 'benefit' comes with the hidden cost of increased Michael exposure — quantified with absurd specificity at 16–18 hours.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '16 to 18 hours' is a nice touch — it sounds like she's calculated this with dread. Good follow-up to joke 1, slightly diminished by being a coda.

jokes.text: In my opinion, the third date is traditionally the one where... You have sex.
jokes.setup: Michael begins a talking-head confessional with 'In my opinion, the third date is traditionally the one where...' in a suspenseful, dramatic tone.
jokes.punchline: He just plainly says 'You have sex.' No euphemism, no buildup — the directness is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup/punchline. The suspenseful lead-in and blunt payoff works, though the actual concept (third date = sex) is a very common trope. Michael's earnestness saves it from being generic.

jokes.text: If she starts having sex with me, I'll know for sure.
jokes.setup: Michael was asked if Holly feels the same way about the third date having significance.
jokes.punchline: Michael's method of confirming Holly's feelings about the third date is empirical — if the sex happens, that confirms it. The logic is both innocent and ridiculous.
jokes.explanation: This is the stronger half of the two-part confessional. The logic is perfectly Michael: naive, self-absorbed, and weirdly scientific. 'I'll know for sure' is a great button. Excellent economy — one sentence does a lot of character work.

jokes.text: - What are you making? - A knife. - You're making a knife with a knife? - You got a better way?
jokes.setup: Jim notices Dwight doing something at his desk and asks what he's making.
jokes.punchline: Dwight is making a knife using a knife as a tool, and when challenged, responds with complete confidence that this is the obvious method.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The premise is absurd but the exchange is perfectly structured: setup, challenge, and Dwight's unshakeable confidence as the punchline. 'You got a better way?' is the ideal button — Dwight isn't being funny, he's being Dwight, which is funnier. Highly quotable and could only come from this character. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in economy and character specificity.

jokes.text: You wanna talk about it? / About what? / You know I know. / You know they know. / I know none of that.
jokes.setup: Jim seems to be probing Dwight about Angela's secret relationship with him while she's engaged to Andy.
jokes.punchline: Dwight denies all knowledge in an increasingly absurd escalation — 'I know none of that. And if I did, you'd be the last to know.'
jokes.explanation: Good layered dialogue. The repetition of 'you know I know / you know they know' builds nicely, and Dwight's 'I know none of that' is a strong denial delivered with perfect Schrute certainty. Rewatch bonus because knowing the Dwight/Angela secret makes it land harder.

jokes.text: Some of what we order depends on if we're having sex after.
jokes.setup: Michael is enthusiastically planning the third-date dinner with Holly, running through food court options like chicken teriyaki vs. hot dog.
jokes.punchline: He casually drops that food selection hinges on whether sex is happening — treating it as a practical logistical variable mid-food-court-planning.
jokes.explanation: Good running gag continuation. The fact that Michael is applying practical caloric logic to romantic planning is perfectly Michael. 'Elephant in the room' that immediately follows lands it well. Character-specific and earned.

jokes.text: Elephant in the room. Are we, do you think? Do you think we're gonna have sex tonight?
jokes.setup: Michael has just noted food selection depends on post-dinner activities. Holly is in the scene.
jokes.punchline: Michael names the 'elephant in the room' and then immediately, earnestly asks Holly directly if they're having sex tonight — no filter, no shame.
jokes.explanation: The cringe is the joke. Michael using the formal 'elephant in the room' framing before asking the bluntest possible question is perfectly in character. The cringe is earned because Holly's presence makes it awkward.

jokes.text: Holly responds 'Hell yeah.' to Michael asking if they're having sex tonight
jokes.setup: Expectation is that Holly will be embarrassed or redirect Michael's blunt question
jokes.punchline: She matches his energy completely — 'Hell yeah' — with zero hesitation
jokes.explanation: Two words do all the work. The misdirect is that we expect social awkwardness; instead Holly proves she's Michael's genuine equal. 'Hell yeah' is perfectly calibrated — enthusiastic, unambiguous, and character-defining for Holly. Excellent economy, great structural placement as the beat that resolves the extended sex-discussion arc.

jokes.text: 'Probably get soup or something light.' — Michael's post-'Hell yeah' date-food recalibration
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly have just enthusiastically confirmed they're having sex tonight
jokes.punchline: Michael's immediate pivot to light pre-sex meal planning — soup — delivered with total pragmatic calm
jokes.explanation: Excellent button to the entire sex-discussion sequence. 'Soup or something light' is Michael being practically romantic — he's following through on his own food logic — and the mundane specificity ('soup') is what makes it funny. Very well-placed, maximum economy.

jokes.text: She introduced me to so many things. Pasteurized milk, sheets, monotheism.
jokes.setup: Dwight is speaking warmly about Angela in a confessional, suggesting she has had a civilizing influence on him.
jokes.punchline: The list of things she introduced him to — pasteurized milk, sheets, monotheism — implies Dwight lived like a feral medieval peasant before Angela.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes, and arguably the best written line. The list escalates perfectly: 'pasteurized milk' (odd but plausible), 'sheets' (concerning), 'monotheism' (completely unhinged). Each item reveals a deeper layer of Dwight's pre-Angela barbarism. Could ONLY be Dwight. The structure is textbook — three-item list with escalating absurdity. Quotable, highly rewatchable, and character-defining. Approaches the 9.5 anchor in quality.

jokes.text: Presents on your birthday, preventative medicine. / - It's nice to learn new things. - I was talking to myself.
jokes.setup: Dwight continues his list of things Angela introduced him to — now 'presents on your birthday' and 'preventative medicine.'
jokes.punchline: Jim offers a sincere-seeming reaction ('It's nice to learn new things'), and Dwight dismisses him: 'I was talking to myself.' The list continues to reveal Dwight's savage baseline, plus Dwight's irritation at Jim's presence.
jokes.explanation: The callback extension of joke 13 works because 'preventative medicine' and 'birthday presents' maintain the absurd logic (Dwight apparently had no sense of self-preservation before Angela). Jim's sincere response and Dwight's 'I was talking to myself' is a perfect beat. The dismissal shows Dwight's self-absorption even in vulnerability.

jokes.text: Why is she marrying Andy? / Angela's not really a risk taker. And Andy's not really a risk.
jokes.setup: Someone questions why Angela is marrying Andy if she seems not to love him.
jokes.punchline: Jim's dry analysis: Angela isn't a risk-taker, and Andy is such a non-threatening choice that he barely qualifies as a 'risk.' The insult to Andy is contained in the logic itself.
jokes.explanation: Elegant double-edged joke. The parallelism ('not really a risk taker / not really a risk') is well-constructed, and the implicit burn on Andy is sharp without being cruel. It also reveals character wisdom — Jim understands Angela. Strong economy.

jokes.text: That's really fattening. / No, it's lettuce.
jokes.setup: Someone comments that what another person is eating is really fattening.
jokes.punchline: The response is simply 'No, it's lettuce' — as if that settles it, delivered as complete authority on the matter.
jokes.explanation: Mildly funny throwaway. Works because of confidence in the response, but there's no real setup and it's not character-specific enough to be memorable. Background gag territory.

jokes.text: I'm a crazy 8. I'm crazy. / You're crazy. Go crazy.
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are goofing off together, apparently with 1 hour 45 minutes before their dinner reservation.
jokes.punchline: Michael declares 'I'm a crazy 8' and both of them fall into a mutual 'crazy' spiral — two people who are equally goofy feeding off each other.
jokes.explanation: The joke is really about the chemistry — two weirdos being weird together. It's charming but not especially crafted. Works more as character/relationship texture than a standalone comedic moment.

jokes.text: Camera look / reaction beat after Holly and Michael go back for his 'keys.'
jokes.setup: Michael says he forgot his keys and they go back inside, but Jim clearly suspects something.
jokes.punchline: Jim's look to camera — a 'can you believe this?' beat as Michael uses a transparent excuse to avoid being caught on camera. Jim knows and the audience knows.
jokes.explanation: Standard mockumentary camera-look beat. Functional but not particularly inventive. Jim's looks are reliable if unexciting.

jokes.text: I didn't forget my keys. I just didn't want to make out with you in front of the cameras.
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly go back inside ostensibly to get his keys.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately admits the keys were a ruse — he just wanted camera-free make-out time. The meta-awareness that they're on a documentary is played for laughs.
jokes.explanation: Good meta-mockumentary joke. Michael showing documentary-awareness while also being completely unselfconscious about why he wants privacy is charming. Sets up the next beat well.

jokes.text: Do you think they can hear us? / Not if we turn these dials all the way down. / Now they can't hear us at all. / Good. We're totally alone.
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly try to get privacy from the documentary crew by turning down audio equipment dials.
jokes.punchline: The audience can STILL hear them perfectly (the show is still airing their conversation), making their belief that they've achieved privacy the joke. 'We're totally alone' is ironic while we watch.
jokes.explanation: Smart meta-mockumentary bit. The characters think they've outsmarted the documentary crew, but we're watching the whole thing. 'We're totally alone' is the ironic button. Works well as a mockumentary-format joke and reveals both characters are equally naive/adorable.

jokes.text: Yes, that's correct. I need to cancel checks from 10,001 to 90,000.
jokes.setup: The office has been robbed. Michael is on the phone dealing with the aftermath.
jokes.punchline: The check range is 10,001 to 90,000 — an absurdly large range that implies Michael has been writing checks with essentially no oversight for a very long time.
jokes.explanation: Strong background detail joke. The specificity of the numbers (80,000 checks!) does the heavy lifting. The joke is in what it implies about Michael's financial chaos without ever saying it directly.

jokes.text: Great, they stole my laptop. / Well, they stole my surge protector. / How does that even compare? / Oscar, I'm now going to be prone to surges.
jokes.setup: Multiple people are listing stolen items. Oscar has lost his laptop.
jokes.punchline: Kevin's complaint about his stolen surge protector — a much cheaper, less critical item — is treated with equal gravity. 'I'm now going to be prone to surges' is delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Kevin's sense of scale is reliably funny. His sincere concern about surge vulnerability is perfect Kevin — not stupid, just operating on his own priority system. 'Prone to surges' is a good line.

jokes.text: Bravo, Watson. / Looks like a classic 7-men job. / Security tapes were stolen. Motives, financial. Or possibly vintage HP computer collectors.
jokes.setup: The office has been robbed and everyone is assessing the damage. Dwight takes it upon himself to investigate.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's detective posturing is absurd: 'classic 7-men job' (no basis), motives are 'financial. Or possibly vintage HP computer collectors' — treating this mundane office robbery like a heist film.
jokes.explanation: Strong Dwight character joke. 'Vintage HP computer collectors' is the best part — it's the kind of hyper-specific, slightly plausible alternative theory only Dwight would float. His detective persona is consistent and well-deployed here.

jokes.text: That wasn't us, right? You remembered to lock the doors? / No, did you? / Michael, I think this is our fault.
jokes.setup: Dwight was just playing detective about the break-in, implying outside forces.
jokes.punchline: Michael and Dwight's private exchange reveals THEY forgot to lock up — meaning Dwight's whole elaborate detective theory was about a crime they enabled.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic callback. Dwight's pompous detective work is undercut immediately by the reveal that he and Michael are at fault. The dramatic irony is well-structured. Rewatch bonus because the detective speech lands differently knowing they did it.

jokes.text: Oh, no. / No, my god! My god. / So much for sex without consequences.
jokes.setup: Michael and Dwight realize the robbery is their fault. Michael is horrified.
jokes.punchline: Michael's reaction to the moral weight of enabling a robbery is 'So much for sex without consequences' — he somehow links the robbery to his sex life, not the financial or legal implications.
jokes.explanation: Excellent character joke with great callback work. Michael's brain immediately translates a workplace crisis into a sexual consequence — which is both absurd and completely in character. The phrase 'sex without consequences' as a concept Michael was apparently anticipating is perfectly Michael Scott. Strong originality in the specific phrase chosen.

jokes.text: Holly calls Michael a dork: 'You are such a dork!'
jokes.setup: Michael says 'so much for sex without consequences'
jokes.punchline: Holly's affectionate 'You are such a dork!' — she finds him charming, not horrifying
jokes.explanation: Functions more as a character beat confirming Holly's affection for Michael than as a joke itself. Not particularly original but serves the scene.

jokes.text: So apparently Pam went out last night and accidentally called my work phone at 3:00 in the morning. I'm on minute six of this message.
jokes.setup: Jim is listening to a voicemail from Pam, who is in New York at art school.
jokes.punchline: Pam apparently left a 6+ minute drunk voicemail to Jim's WORK phone at 3 AM — the specifics (work phone, six minutes, 3 AM) all compound the embarrassment.
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy. The specifics do the work — the six-minute duration and the work phone (not his cell) suggest Pam is both very drunk and not entirely lucid. Warmly funny rather than mean.

jokes.text: You can take the girl out of Philly. / Scranton.
jokes.setup: Jim makes a 'you can take the girl out of Philly' comment about drunk Pam.
jokes.punchline: Jim is corrected — Pam is from Scranton, not Philly. Jim immediately accepts the correction, meaning his whole 'worldly city girl going wild' framing collapses. Scranton is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: Economy joke. 'Scranton' as the one-word correction-punchline deflates Jim's romantic framing perfectly. The comedy is in how mundane 'Scranton' sounds versus 'Philly.' Simple and effective.

jokes.text: The future mother of my children.
jokes.setup: Jim has just played a clip of Pam drunk-denying being drunk at 3 AM on a work voicemail.
jokes.punchline: Jim's fond, sincere label — 'the future mother of my children' — applied to this chaotic moment is the joke. It's affectionate teasing that reveals Jim's genuine love for Pam.
jokes.explanation: Warm, character-rich punchline. The contrast between 'the future mother of my children' as a dignified label and the chaos of the drunk voicemail is beautifully understated. It's romantic without being saccharine. Strong character integration — only Jim would respond to Pam's most embarrassing moment with sincere affection.

jokes.text: I never felt safe here. / You're always safe with me. I'm a very good screamer.
jokes.setup: In the aftermath of the robbery, Holly says she never felt safe at the office.
jokes.punchline: Michael's reassurance that she's safe with him — 'I'm a very good screamer' — is the joke. The reassurance is simultaneously sincere and absurd (screaming is not a security measure).
jokes.explanation: Solid Michael joke. 'I'm a very good screamer' as a security credential is absurd but completely in character — Michael genuinely believes this is reassuring. Good economy.

jokes.text: And one day, we're gonna move to Disney's celebration village in Florida and leave all of this behind. / I would very much like that.
jokes.setup: Michael is comforting Holly after the robbery.
jokes.punchline: Michael's vision of the future is 'Disney's Celebration Village in Florida' — a real planned Disney community, but absurdly specific and suburban as a romantic dream. Holly's sincere 'I would very much like that' makes it sweeter and funnier.
jokes.explanation: Lovely character moment. 'Disney's Celebration Village' is a surprisingly specific and deeply Michael Scott dream — corporate, optimistic, infantile. Holly's genuine enthusiasm for this dream is what makes it work — she's the right person for him. Rewatch bonus because it foreshadows their eventual relationship trajectory.

jokes.text: Dwight's mysterious 'Get in.' — pulling up in a car or vehicle to apparently take action on the Angela situation
jokes.setup: Dwight is dealing with the Angela/Andy situation
jokes.punchline: The terse, action-movie 'Get in.' delivery for what is clearly an office drama situation
jokes.explanation: Two words that communicate Dwight's delusion about his own importance. The action-movie register applied to a workplace romance subplot is the joke. Economy is the main asset.

jokes.text: Then you need to give her an ultimatum. Tell her she needs to make a choice. You or Andy. / It did when Bob said I had to stop talking to my sister on the phone so much.
jokes.setup: Phyllis is advising Dwight on how to handle Angela (who is engaged to Andy but secretly with Dwight). She suggests an ultimatum.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's proof that ultimatums work is that her husband Bob made her stop calling her sister — presenting an example of her own subjugation as relationship advice success.
jokes.explanation: Sharp Phyllis character joke. The dark subtext — that Phyllis's example of an ultimatum working is one where she was the one controlled — is played completely straight. The joke works because Phyllis is oblivious to the irony. Strong character integration and earned.

jokes.text: Wait, this isn't our floor, Dwight.
jokes.setup: Dwight has led Phyllis to a private area to have a secret conversation.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's realization that they're on the wrong floor — delivered as a non-sequitur — reveals that Dwight has been so caught up in his scheming that he's literally gotten lost.
jokes.explanation: Minor background gag. The joke is in the mundane wrongness of the location, suggesting Dwight's dramatic scheming hasn't even gotten the basics right. Not especially crafted but functional.

jokes.text: How's everyone doing? My door is always open if anyone wants to talk.
jokes.setup: The office has just been robbed. Employees are stressed and upset about missing items.
jokes.punchline: Michael breezes in with generic motivational manager platitudes as if the situation is a minor morale issue rather than an actual crime.
jokes.explanation: Standard Michael manager-obliviousness joke. Functional but a familiar beat in The Office's playbook. Doesn't add much beyond establishing Michael's characteristic tone-deafness.

jokes.text: I don't want to talk. I want my laptop back.
jokes.setup: Michael offers his open door for anyone who 'wants to talk' after the robbery.
jokes.punchline: Oscar's blunt correction — he doesn't need emotional support, he needs his laptop — is the straight-man response to Michael's hollow platitude.
jokes.explanation: Good economy. Oscar's directness is always reliable as a comedy element, and this response cleanly undercuts Michael's performative concern. Short and effective.

jokes.text: Creed's talking-head: 'Nobody steals from Creed Bratton and gets away with it. The last person to do this disappeared. His name? Creed Bratton.'
jokes.setup: Creed declares nobody steals from him and gets away with it
jokes.punchline: The last thief 'disappeared' — then he reveals the thief's name was also Creed Bratton, implying he stole from himself or that 'Creed Bratton' is an assumed identity after doing something criminal
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the best Creed moments in the entire series. The structure is perfect: confident threat → dark revelation → name twist that implies Creed stole his own identity (or literally committed a crime and fled under a new name). It's entirely in character — Creed exists in a universe of implied crimes and assumed identities — and it escalates from a cliché tough-guy line to genuine menace in two sentences. The 'His name? Creed Bratton.' construction (the rhetorical question to himself) is immaculate. Highly quotable, extremely rewatch-worthy, and absolutely could not come from any other character on any other show.

jokes.text: Nobody steals from Creed Bratton and gets away with it. The last person to do this disappeared. His name? Creed Bratton.
jokes.setup: Creed announces that nobody steals from him and gets away with it, threatening consequences for the robbers.
jokes.punchline: The last person to steal from Creed... was Creed himself. He disappeared. The implication: Creed either killed himself, faked his own death, or has multiple identities. Delivered completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and one of The Office's all-time great Creed moments. The structure is flawless: threatening setup, the pause before 'His name?', and then the utterly deranged self-referential answer. It works on every level — it's dark, absurd, perfectly economic, and could ONLY be Creed Bratton. The joke reveals Creed's entire character in two sentences: he's a criminal, possibly a fugitive, possibly deranged, and completely unaware of how alarming he is. Approaches the 9.5 craft anchor. Quotability is essentially 10 — this line is a cultural touchstone within the show's fandom.

jokes.text: I'm calling it Crime Aid. It's like Farm Aid. But instead of farms fighting against aids, it is us fighting against our own poverty.
jokes.setup: Michael proposes a charity auction to recoup stolen items and explains the name 'Crime Aid.'
jokes.punchline: Michael's explanation of Farm Aid — 'farms fighting against aids' — is both incorrect and a completely wrong understanding of what Farm Aid is. His pivot to 'our own poverty' is also unintentionally accurate.
jokes.explanation: Good Michael joke. 'Farms fighting against aids' is a genuine misunderstanding delivered with confidence — Michael doesn't know what Farm Aid is but isn't going to let that stop him. 'Our own poverty' as a self-deprecating pivot is also funny. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Was this a sorority that you didn't get into a real sorority so you had to kind of form your own?
jokes.setup: Kelly (or Meredith) mentions her sorority used to do charity auctions. Michael asks about it.
jokes.punchline: Michael interrupts to ask if it was a 'fake' sorority formed because she couldn't get into a real one — a casually cruel assumption delivered as a neutral clarifying question.
jokes.explanation: Classic Michael obtuse cruelty. The question is genuinely mean but Michael has no awareness of that — he's asking as if it's a totally normal thing to inquire about. Character-specific and well-integrated.

jokes.text: We'll auction off people, like in the olden days.
jokes.setup: Michael is brainstorming auction ideas, building excitement for the Crime Aid event.
jokes.punchline: Michael suggests auctioning off people 'like in the olden days' — an offhand slavery reference delivered with complete obliviousness.
jokes.explanation: Michael's casual obliviousness to dark historical references is a recurring bit. This is a lighter version of it — the joke lands but it's not particularly inventive. 'In the olden days' softens and slightly muddles the punchline.

jokes.text: So, in order to recoup the value of items we liked, we have to spend more money on things we don't want. Who would ever come to this?
jokes.setup: Michael has just pitched the Crime Aid auction as a great idea.
jokes.punchline: Oscar's cold logical analysis of the auction's fundamental flaw — you spend money to get back money you lost — delivered flatly.
jokes.explanation: Good Oscar straight-man joke. His accounting brain immediately spots the logical flaw in Michael's plan. 'Who would ever come to this?' is a strong button. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: It could be a pedestrian. It could be an old person. It could be a lookie-loo.
jokes.setup: Oscar asks who would attend this charity auction.
jokes.punchline: Michael lists possible attendees — 'a pedestrian,' 'an old person,' 'a lookie-loo' — as if these are compelling demographic targets for an event.
jokes.explanation: 'Lookie-loo' as a target market is the best element — it's a non-category. Michael's audience brainstorm reveals he has no actual plan. 'Pedestrian' is also funny as the most optimistic possible walk-in demographic.

jokes.text: Michael's long rambling non-sequitur about Bruce Springsteen ending in 'I think it is very apparent... There's a point there. But what is the point?' followed by 'Do you need us for any of this? / Do I?'
jokes.setup: Michael seems to be building to a reveal about a special auction item, but his teasing goes on incomprehensibly long.
jokes.punchline: Michael loses the thread of his own reveal mid-monologue, questioning himself out loud ('what is the point?'), and then the employees just ask if they're needed — which Michael also can't answer.
jokes.explanation: The joke is Michael's meandering — but it runs a bit long in the transcript. The payoff ('Do I?') is good, but the extended rambling tests patience. Character-specific but not well-edited. Loses points for economy.

jokes.text: Michael scored the big ticket item. Springsteen tickets. The boss scored the boss. I think that's pretty boss. He knows how to get things. He got me.
jokes.setup: Holly is doing a talking-head about Michael's acquisition of Springsteen tickets for Crime Aid.
jokes.punchline: Holly works 'boss' three ways — Bruce Springsteen's nickname, general slang for cool, and as a compliment to Michael — then caps it with the sincere 'He got me,' which is both a pun on acquisition and a romantic declaration.
jokes.explanation: Clever Holly moment. The triple use of 'boss' is well-constructed wordplay that also reveals character — Holly is nerdy and enthusiastic in the same key as Michael. 'He got me' as the romantic button is sweet and slightly self-aware. Strong structure for a talking head.

jokes.text: Holly's awkward camera look after Michael's 'Sorry. Twice. Right?' — implying she's been embarrassed by him twice already this morning
jokes.setup: Michael has just delivered his typically chaotic and self-aggrandizing Springsteen pitch
jokes.punchline: Holly does an awkward camera acknowledgment — 'Sorry. Twice. Right?' from Michael suggests she's had to apologize for him at least twice in a short period
jokes.explanation: A subtle beat that plays on the new-relationship dynamic — Holly is still figuring out that with Michael, you apologize frequently. 'Twice. Right?' from Michael suggesting he's keeping count is a good detail.

jokes.text: Listen to me close cause I'm only gonna say this once. You either break off your engagement with that singing buffoon, apologize, and then date me. Or you can say goodbye to this.
jokes.setup: Dwight has decided to give Angela an ultimatum about choosing between him and Andy.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's ultimatum is theatrically intense but also deeply self-undermining — 'goodbye to this' implies Angela should want him so badly she'll leave her fiancé, but 'this' is Dwight. Also, 'singing buffoon' for Andy is a great small burn.
jokes.explanation: Good Dwight ultimatum joke. 'Singing buffoon' is sharp for Andy (who does sing constantly). The whole setup — presenting himself as an irresistible alternative — is delusional in a perfectly Dwight way.

jokes.text: I think you have me confused with another person. / I said I was only gonna say it once.
jokes.setup: After Dwight's dramatic ultimatum, Angela responds dismissively.
jokes.punchline: Angela's flat denial ('I think you have me confused with another person') followed by Dwight's insistence that he already said his piece — he's given his ultimatum and won't repeat it even to clarify the confusion — is absurd Dwight logic.
jokes.explanation: The callback to 'I was only gonna say it once' as a reason to not repeat himself even when the whole ultimatum has been miscommunicated is very Dwight — he'd rather lose than break his own arbitrary rule.

jokes.text: You have until 6:14 P.M. / 6:14. / I heard you. / Pump it up!
jokes.setup: Dwight sets a deadline for Angela's decision on his ultimatum.
jokes.punchline: The specificity of 6:14 (not 6:00, not 6:30 — 6:14) is absurd, and Dwight immediately pivoting to 'Pump it up!' as he exits is either an involuntary release valve or a bizarre attempt at confidence.
jokes.explanation: 6:14 as a deadline is perfectly Dwight — arbitrary hyper-specificity in a completely inappropriate context. 'Pump it up!' as a kicker is wonderfully bizarre. The combination is the joke.

jokes.text: And welcome to C.R.I.M.E.-A.I.D. / Crime Reduces Innocence Makes Everyone Angry, I Declare.
jokes.setup: Michael introduces Crime Aid as a formal event, giving it an acronym breakdown.
jokes.punchline: The backronym is grammatically tortured — 'I Declare' just to make it fit — and 'Crime Reduces Innocence Makes Everyone Angry' is a barely coherent sentence. Michael is clearly very proud of it.
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed Michael joke. The backronym genre is inherently funny, and 'I Declare' as the end cap — clearly forced to complete the acronym — is a great small detail. Michael's formality about a completely ridiculous construction is perfect character work.

jokes.text: It is not known how many office robberies occur every second, cause there is no wikipedia entry for office robbery statistics.
jokes.setup: Michael is giving an opening speech for Crime Aid, trying to establish the gravity of office robbery.
jokes.punchline: Michael cites the absence of a Wikipedia article as the reason a statistic is unknown — Wikipedia is his primary research source, and he admits it.
jokes.explanation: Sharp character joke. The logic is specific and perfectly Michael — he's not making up a statistic, he's explaining why he CAN'T cite one, and the reason is that Wikipedia failed him. This is a great satirical note on early-2000s/late-2000s Wikipedia culture and Michael's research habits. Strong economy.

jokes.text: Mike gave me a list of his top ten Springsteen songs. 3 of them were Huey Lewis and the News. One was Tracy Chapman, Fast Car. And my personal favorite, Short People.
jokes.setup: A Springsteen-adjacent musician (or the real Springsteen, context unclear) describes the list Michael gave him of top 10 Springsteen songs.
jokes.punchline: Michael's list includes songs by three different artists, none of whom are Springsteen. The escalating wrongness (Huey Lewis, Tracy Chapman, then 'Short People' by Randy Newman) is perfectly calibrated.
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke. The three-item escalating list structure is perfect: 3 Huey Lewis songs (worrying), Tracy Chapman's Fast Car (quite different from Springsteen, more concerning), and then 'Short People' (not even by any of the above artists, completely left field). The final item is the laugh — 'Short People' by Randy Newman is such a specific, random choice that it perfectly encapsulates Michael's musical confusion. Strong structure, high originality, and deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: Michael auctions Holly's yoga lesson starting at $300, calling it 'very boss indeed,' and then immediately bids and wins at $300 himself
jokes.setup: Michael is auctioning Holly's yoga lesson with great enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Nobody else bids, so Michael buys it himself — he outbid nobody to buy his girlfriend's services from his own auction
jokes.explanation: The joke has good structure — Michael's auctioneer energy and the complete failure of the auction collapse in one beat. 'Sold for $300 to me!' delivered with triumph despite obvious embarrassment is character-specific.

jokes.text: Sold for $300 to me! / What the hell is that? / It's the only gavel I could find. It squeaks when you bang it. That's what she said.
jokes.setup: Michael is auctioneering and gavels the first sale — but the gavel is a rubber toy that squeaks.
jokes.punchline: Michael immediately does a 'That's what she said' on his own explanation of the squeaking gavel — reflexive, unprompted, and completely without shame.
jokes.explanation: The 'That's what she said' is a classic Michael running gag. This instance is functional — the setup is decent (the squeaking gavel genuinely lends itself to it) — but it's not a particularly inspired use of the trope. The visual gag of the squeaky gavel is the stronger element.

jokes.text: Darryl and the boys in the hood in the warehouse have graciously donated... go out for a beer with them right now.
jokes.setup: Michael is describing the warehouse workers' donation to the auction.
jokes.punchline: 'Boys in the hood' — a casually inappropriate racial coding of Darryl and the warehouse workers. Michael is oblivious to the term's connotations.
jokes.explanation: Michael's racial obliviousness is a recurring element. This is a gentler version — he's not being intentionally offensive, just carelessly using loaded language. Character-specific but not the show's most nuanced use of this dynamic.

jokes.text: You know what? I'm actually going to bid on this. I'm gonna start the bidding cause this is something that I've dreamt of. / Mike, you can't do this. It's conflict of interest. / $5. / Sold to Jim!
jokes.setup: The 'go for a beer with the warehouse guys' lot is up for auction. Michael wants to bid despite being the auctioneer.
jokes.punchline: Jim warns him it's conflict of interest, Michael ignores it and bids $5, and Jim immediately gavels it sold — in complete solidarity with getting Michael out of the auction and into the beer situation.
jokes.explanation: Good bit. Jim's immediate 'Sold to Jim!' after warning Michael is funny — Jim is not actually opposed to the conflict of interest, he just wanted to go on record. The collaboration between Jim enabling Michael's chaos is reliable comedy.

jokes.text: Well, this next item is sure to spring steam from your ears if you don't win it. / It just says Creed. / Yeah, that's all-inclusive.
jokes.setup: Michael introduces the next auction item with his usual baroque teasing.
jokes.punchline: The item is just 'Creed' — whatever Creed decides to provide is the lot. 'All-inclusive' means nothing specific has been promised, which is either terrifying or meaningless.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Creed joke. 'Just Creed. All-inclusive.' is perfect — it implies Creed was so enigmatic or unreliable that even he couldn't specify what he'd offer. The joke is in the complete blankness of the auction lot and the horror/intrigue that implies. Very Creed.

jokes.text: She thought I was McNabb. / I can see that.
jokes.setup: Darryl and Roy are at the bar. Darryl is describing a mistaken identity moment — presumably a woman thought he was Eagles QB Donovan McNabb.
jokes.punchline: Roy's 'I can see that' is deadpan validation — either he genuinely thinks Darryl looks like McNabb or he's being a good wingman. Either reading is funny.
jokes.explanation: Serviceable background joke. Roy's two-word response is the strength — 'I can see that' works because of its flatness. Limited setup context from the transcript makes it harder to evaluate fully.

jokes.text: I'm Kevin. And I'll do your taxes. / Kevin the taxman. / Federal and state.
jokes.setup: Kevin's auction item is that he will do your taxes. He introduces himself as if the name 'Kevin' isn't enough.
jokes.punchline: 'I'm Kevin' as an introduction (as if that clarifies things) followed by 'Federal and state' as an added selling point for his tax service — Kevin treating this like a business pitch with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: Good Kevin joke. The self-introduction as if 'Kevin' is a selling point, the pitch structure of 'federal and state,' and the crowd's enthusiastic 'Kevin the taxman!' echo make this a fun bit. Kevin's sincere professional pride in his tax knowledge is reliably funny.

jokes.text: You know what? I would appreciate it if people would stop storming off the stage.
jokes.setup: Multiple auction items have apparently gone badly — someone has dramatically left the stage mid-lot.
jokes.punchline: Michael's mild-mannered complaint about repeated stage-storming — 'I would appreciate it' — implies this has now happened multiple times, and his tone is that of a long-suffering host.
jokes.explanation: Good background joke. The implication that stage-storming has become a recurring problem at this auction is funny without being explicit. 'I would appreciate it' as a formal complaint is very Michael's passive-aggressive register.

jokes.text: We are getting there folks. Slow and steady.
jokes.setup: The Crime Aid auction is apparently not going well — the event has clearly been chaotic.
jokes.punchline: Michael's optimistic 'slow and steady' framing for what appears to be a disaster-in-progress is the joke — he's still projecting confidence despite evident chaos.
jokes.explanation: Minor filler joke. Michael's relentless positivity in adversity is a reliable note, but 'slow and steady' isn't a particularly inventive expression of it. Functional but lightweight.

jokes.text: I'd like to auction off a weekend at my place in Martha's Vineyard. / $100. / Great.
jokes.setup: Corporate CFO David Wallace shows up and offers a weekend at his Martha's Vineyard property.
jokes.punchline: The first bid is $100 for a Martha's Vineyard weekend — absurdly low for what that implies. 'Great' from Wallace suggests he's just happy anyone bid at all.
jokes.explanation: Mild joke relying on the contrast between the value of the item and the opening bid. Works as a note about the event's overall failure. Not especially memorable.

jokes.text: Phyllis, someone let the air out of your tires. Come quick.
jokes.setup: The Martha's Vineyard bidding is happening, building toward a good total.
jokes.punchline: Dwight interrupts the auction to lure Phyllis away by claiming someone let the air out of her tires — he actually did this himself to get rid of Phyllis so he can proceed with his Angela plan.
jokes.explanation: Strong Dwight joke. The casualness of the sabotage — he literally deflated her tires just to have a conversation — is perfectly Dwight. The reveal ('Why couldn't you just said it? Why did you actually do it?') makes it funnier. Dwight's willingness to commit petty sabotage for personal scheming is deeply in character.

jokes.text: Why couldn't you just said it? Why did you actually do it?
jokes.setup: Dwight claims someone let the air out of Phyllis's tires to lure her away.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis realizes Dwight actually did it — and her question ('Why did you actually DO it?') reveals she understood that Dwight could have just lied, but he went ahead and committed actual vandalism.
jokes.explanation: Great Phyllis reaction. The key insight — 'Why did you ACTUALLY do it?' — reveals that Phyllis is smarter than she looks; she immediately clocks that Dwight escalated from a lie to real vandalism unnecessarily. This is a great straight-man line that also characterizes both Dwight's impracticality and Phyllis's underrated perception.

jokes.text: I just think we all deserve to be with someone who wants to be with us.
jokes.setup: Dwight asks Phyllis for her 'big master plan' to win Angela back after the ultimatum failed.
jokes.punchline: Phyllis's advice is genuinely wise and sincere — 'we all deserve to be with someone who wants to be with us' — completely subverting the expectation of a scheming strategy. The joke is Dwight's inability to accept simple wisdom.
jokes.explanation: Nice Phyllis moment. The joke works because the subversion is Phyllis being genuinely insightful, which neither Dwight nor the audience expected. Dwight's rejection of the good advice (he immediately looks for a workaround) is the character beat.

jokes.text: I get it. You're trying to secure your place as head of the party-planning committee. You're just being selfish.
jokes.setup: Phyllis has just given Dwight genuinely good relationship advice.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's mind cannot process sincere altruism — so he invents a self-serving motive for Phyllis's kindness (she wants to secure her party-planning committee position). The delusion is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Dwight character joke. The party-planning committee connection is so random and specific that it perfectly encapsulates how Dwight's paranoid worldview works — he can't accept kindness, so he manufactures a conspiracy. Very quotable and character-defining.

jokes.text: And you slap like a girl.
jokes.setup: Dwight is angry at Phyllis for her 'selfish' advice and apparently Phyllis slapped him (inferred from context).
jokes.punchline: Dwight's parting shot — 'you slap like a girl' — is petulant and also very Dwight (he'd take a slap as a point of pride, so critiquing the technique is his revenge).
jokes.explanation: Minor joke. Works on economy — five words and it's done. Dwight critiquing Phyllis's slap technique as if it's a skill gap rather than reacting to the insult is character-specific. Not the episode's strongest moment but functional.

jokes.text: What did Phyllis do wrong? I'll tell you what Phyllis did wrong. She stuck her nose into my business and tried to help me.
jokes.setup: Dwight is in a confessional, reflecting on his interaction with Phyllis.
jokes.punchline: Dwight's grievance against Phyllis is that she 'tried to help' him — he frames unsolicited sincere help as a violation. The self-awareness-free delivery is the punchline.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The structure is perfect: the mock-indignant rhetorical question ('What did Phyllis do wrong?'), the dramatic pause, and the punchline that what she did wrong was attempt kindness. The joke works because Dwight means it completely sincerely — trying to help him IS an offense in his worldview. Highly quotable, strong character integration. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

jokes.text: Jim casually tells Roy: 'She's engaged... to me.' — beat between 'engaged' and 'to me'
jokes.setup: Roy asks how Pam is doing; Jim shares updates including art school
jokes.punchline: Jim lands 'She's engaged' — a pause that lets Roy think she's engaged to someone else — then 'to me,' delivered with quiet satisfaction
jokes.explanation: An expertly constructed comedic beat. The pause between 'engaged' and 'to me' is everything — it lets Roy (and the audience) process the wrong interpretation for just a second. The economy is nearly perfect: three words do complex emotional work (closure on the Jim/Roy rivalry, Jim's satisfaction, Roy's deflation). The awkward silence IS the joke. This is Jim deploying understated wit at its best.

jokes.text: She's engaged... to me.
jokes.setup: Jim tells Roy that Pam is in New York, doing well, loves her classes, loves the city. Roy seems wistful.
jokes.punchline: Jim pauses after 'She's engaged...' — letting Roy think for a moment — before adding 'to me.' The timing-based misdirection is the joke, played completely deadpan.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout moments. The structure is near-perfect: Jim gives Roy a full rundown of how great Pam is doing, drops 'She's engaged' — letting Roy think for a beat — and then lands 'to me.' Economy is a 10: two words and a pause tell the whole story. The beat works because of the Jim/Roy/Pam history, making it deeply character-specific. Jim's subtle satisfaction in delivering this news (and his tact in not gloating) is all embedded in the delivery. Strong quotability — 'She's engaged... to me' is a classically Jim line.

jokes.text: Last night, she was out with her friends till like, 8:00 A.M. / What?
jokes.setup: Jim is telling Roy how great Pam is doing — loves her classes, loves the city.
jokes.punchline: Jim drops '8:00 AM' as an afterthought about Pam's social life, and Roy's 'What?' captures the exact moment both men realize Jim may have revealed something that complicates his confidence.
jokes.explanation: Good timing joke. Jim's casual mention of 8 AM and Roy's 'What?' creates a brief shared moment of 'wait, is everything actually fine?' The joke is that Jim, who just won the Pam situation, now has to absorb this information in front of Roy. The dynamic is character-rich.

jokes.text: I am going to see Pam. Because... I feel like I should.
jokes.setup: Roy hears that Pam was out with friends until 8 AM.
jokes.punchline: Roy decides to go see Pam — his stated reason ('I feel like I should') is deliberately vague, but the implication (Jim just revealed something that makes Roy think an opening exists) is clear.
jokes.explanation: Mild joke — more of a character beat than a punchline. Roy's delusional opportunism ('I feel like I should') is the joke, but it requires context to land fully. Functional for plot but not a strong standalone comedy moment.

jokes.text: Has anyone seen an envelope with Bruce Springsteen front row tickets and backstage passes? / Do you want us to look for them? / No. I think they were stolen. I think they were stolen and they're gone forever.
jokes.setup: Michael announces the big ticket item — Springsteen front row tickets — and then immediately can't find them.
jokes.punchline: When offered help finding the tickets, Michael declines — he's already decided they're gone forever. The fatalism is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good Michael joke. His immediate surrender ('they're gone forever') after a cursory check is very Michael — the leap from 'I can't find them right now' to 'stolen and gone forever' with no investigation is perfectly in character. The offered help he refuses is a nice touch.

jokes.text: That was the last good item. So... good job, everybody.
jokes.setup: The Springsteen tickets are gone, ending the Crime Aid auction without its marquee item.
jokes.punchline: Michael wraps the auction with 'So... good job, everybody' — a hollow congratulation for a failed event, delivered with what sounds like genuine attempt at positivity.
jokes.explanation: Good economy. 'Good job, everybody' as a conclusion to a chaotic failed auction is a deadpan button. Michael's inability to admit defeat while also clearly defeated is the character note.

jokes.text: Well, Phyllis, nobody really wants a hug, so. / I'll bid on a hug. / She's your wife, you idiot.
jokes.setup: Phyllis's auction item — a hug — is dismissed by Michael. Bob Vance immediately bids.
jokes.punchline: Someone points out that Bob is bidding on a hug from his own wife — 'She's your wife, you idiot' — which is both a criticism and also kind of sweet.
jokes.explanation: Good Bob Vance joke. The fact that Bob bids on his own wife's hug is both romantic and slightly absurd — it sets up the escalating bidding war that follows. 'She's your wife, you idiot' is a strong straight-man line.

jokes.text: The Phyllis hug bidding war: escalating from $300 to $350 to $400 to $500, with 'and one penny' added each round, culminating in '$1 million' then settling at $1,000.
jokes.setup: The bidding on Phyllis's hug has become a war between Michael and Bob Vance, with someone adding 'and one penny' to every bid.
jokes.punchline: The absurdity of bidding $1,000 for a hug from Phyllis — driven partly by 'and one penny' gamesmanship and partly by Michael's desperate need for affection — is the sustained joke. '$1 million' as an overcorrection bid is the peak.
jokes.explanation: Good sustained escalation sequence. The 'and one penny' move is a genuinely clever auction tactic played for absurdity. The whole sequence works because Michael's desperate need for a hug from Phyllis — when Holly is right there — reveals his emotional state. Could run slightly leaner.

jokes.text: No. You know what? No. Because... I'm not that guy. And... we are not that couple.
jokes.setup: After Roy's comment about seeing Pam, Jim has a private confessional moment.
jokes.punchline: Jim deciding, on camera, to NOT go to New York to check on Pam — despite being visibly bothered by the 8 AM revelation — and asserting 'I'm not that guy / we are not that couple' is played as a sincere character moment, but the comedy is in his need to say it at all.
jokes.explanation: Good Jim confessional. The comedy is subtle — Jim insisting he's not going to be the jealous boyfriend while clearly wrestling with jealousy. 'We are not that couple' as a declaration reveals that he's had to remind himself of this. Warm character moment with comedic undertone.

jokes.text: Listen, about the tickets. It's sort of a gray... kind of a gray area in terms of whether I had them.
jokes.setup: The Springsteen tickets went missing at the auction. Michael addresses what happened.
jokes.punchline: Michael's admission that it's a 'gray area' whether he 'had' the tickets implies he never actually had confirmed tickets — he possibly just claimed to have them and hoped it would work out.
jokes.explanation: Strong Michael confession joke. 'A gray area in terms of whether I had them' is a beautifully evasive non-admission. The implication (Michael doesn't actually have the tickets) is devastating, and his casual framing as a 'gray area' rather than 'I lied' is perfect Michael rationalization.

jokes.text: The Springsteen tickets seemed too good to be true. / But a lot of Michael seems too good to be true. / So far it's all true. / But yeah, those tickets really seemed too good to be true.
jokes.setup: Holly is reflecting on Michael getting Springsteen tickets in a confessional.
jokes.punchline: Holly's logic: Michael as a whole seems too good to be true, but he's delivered so far — so maybe the tickets were real? Then immediately: 'But yeah, those tickets really seemed too good to be true.' She can't quite commit to the faith.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Holly confessional. The structure is layered: she builds a logical argument that Michael is genuine ('so far it's all true'), then immediately walks it back with 'but yeah, those tickets really seemed too good to be true.' The self-contradiction is the joke, and it's sweet because it shows Holly is genuinely trying to believe in Michael. Strong structure and character integration. Well-crafted.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking-head: 'The Springsteen tickets seemed too good to be true. But a lot of Michael seems too good to be true. So far it's all true. But yeah, those tickets really seemed too good to be true.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is reflecting on the tickets situation
jokes.punchline: Kevin's logic meanders — he defends Michael's general track record ('so far it's all true') then concludes the tickets were specifically too good to be true — a circular non-conclusion that perfectly captures Kevin's cognition
jokes.explanation: Kevin's rambling talking-head perfectly captures his thought process — he builds toward a conclusion, defends Michael, then arrives back where he started. 'So far it's all true' as a qualifier is the best line, implying Kevin has been monitoring Michael's truthfulness like a portfolio.

jokes.text: No. I did not know that Michael was dating Holly.
jokes.setup: End-of-episode confessional in which a coworker is asked about Michael and Holly's relationship.
jokes.punchline: The flat denial — with the implication that everyone knew and this person is clearly lying/oblivious — is a classic mockumentary button. The delivery of 'No. I did not know that' with the period-pause suggests they knew exactly.
jokes.explanation: Standard mockumentary tag joke. Works as a button but is a familiar format for The Office's endings. Not especially inventive, but appropriate as a closing beat.

tmdb_overview: Michael and Holly have sex for the first time, and Michael holds a fund-raiser for the office after it is burglarized. Dwight confides in Phyllis after Andy and Angela set a wedding date, and Jim runs into Pam's ex-fiancé Roy.
